record.paper_title: Semantic Subtyping: Challenges, Perspectives, and Open Problems
record.original_question: In semantic-subtyping-based systems such as the lambda-calculus system Duce and the pi-calculus system π, deciding subtyping appears to require deciding whether certain denotable types are atomic, or more generally whether a type contains finitely many atomic types that can be enumerated. What mathematical phenomenon makes atomic types arise so persistently in semantic subtyping, how tightly is the semantic-subtyping technique tied to decidability of atomicity, and is it reasonable and possible to study semantic-subtyping systems in which atomic types are not denotable and the subtype lattice is dense?

evidence.quote: Since these atomic types pop out so frequently a first challenge is understanding why this happens and therefore how much the semantic subtyping technique is tightened to the decidability of atomicity. In particular, we may wonder whether it is reasonable and possible to study systems in which atomic types are not denotable so that the set of subtypes of a type is dense.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. In the semantic-subtyping approach to designing type systems, types are interpreted as subsets of a model D, and subtyping S ≤ T is defined to hold exactly when the interpretation of S is contained in the interpretation of T. The type language is closed under the boolean connectives (union, intersection, and negation), so the set of denotable types forms a boolean algebra (modulo semantic equivalence) and the subtyping relation is the induced lattice order. A denotable type T is called atomic if T is not equivalent to the empty type and the only denotable subtypes of T are T itself and the empty type; equivalently, T is a minimal nonzero element of the subtype lattice. Concrete instances include the lambda-calculus system "CDuce" and pi-calculus systems based on semantic subtyping, in which deciding S ≤ T is reduced to emptiness checks that, in known decidability proofs, ultimately rely on enumerating the (finitely many) atomic types contained in a denotable type.

Problem. Provide a mathematical explanation of the following three intertwined questions about semantic-subtyping systems whose type interpretation lies in a model D as above.

(1) Identify the structural phenomenon that forces the recurrent appearance of atomic types in semantic-subtyping decision procedures: characterize, in terms of properties of the model D and of the boolean algebra of denotable types (e.g. atomicity, atomicness, completeness, descending chain conditions, definability of singletons, or finite-model properties), why every currently known decidability proof for semantic subtyping reduces to enumerating atoms of denotable types.

(2) Determine how tightly the semantic-subtyping technique is tied to the decidability of atomicity: exhibit either a general theorem showing that decidability of S ≤ T in a semantic-subtyping system implies decidability of "is T atomic?" (and effectiveness of an enumeration of the atoms below T), or a counterexample consisting of a semantic-subtyping system with decidable subtyping in which atomicity of denotable types is undecidable or in which atoms cannot be effectively enumerated.

(3) Construct, if possible, a non-trivial semantic-subtyping system in which no denotable type is atomic — equivalently, in which the subtype lattice (restricted to nonempty denotable types) is dense, meaning that whenever S < T are denotable and S is not equivalent to the empty type, there exists a denotable U with S < U < T — while still admitting a sound and decidable subtyping algorithm for a useful programming-language type discipline (covering, e.g., product, function, and recursive types). Alternatively, prove that no such system can exist under reasonable expressiveness assumptions.
artifact.status_search_result: The questions are posed as conceptual open challenges about semantic subtyping. Subsequent work has refined decidability results for semantic subtyping with type variables (e.g. EXPTIME decidability by Castagna et al., and logical/tableau approaches), but no source located addresses the specific structural question of why atomic types are unavoidable, or constructs a semantic-subtyping system whose subtype lattice is dense (no denotable atoms). The status of these questions therefore appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Semantic subtyping: challenges, perspectives, and open problems
status_evidence.snippet: Atomic types pop out so frequently; understanding why this happens and how much the technique is tied to decidability of atomicity remains a challenge; one may ask whether systems with non-denotable atoms and dense subtype lattices are possible.
status_evidence.claim: The questions about atomic types and density of the subtype lattice are explicitly listed as challenges/open problems.

status_evidence.title: A Logical Approach to Deciding Semantic Subtyping
status_evidence.snippet: Decidability of subtyping is approached via logical encoding; atomic/singleton types still play a central role in known decision procedures.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent decidability work continues to rely on atom-like reasoning, and does not resolve the dense-lattice question.

status_evidence.title: Complexity of Subtype Satisfiability over Posets
status_evidence.snippet: Subtype satisfiability is well understood when atomic types form a lattice, but little is known beyond that.
status_evidence.claim: Indicates that the role of atoms in subtyping decision problems is central and not fully understood in non-lattice or dense settings.
